content:
The kitchen is one of the busiest rooms and one of the riskiest.

This guide covers practical changes. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Layout

  • Keep everyday items between waist and shoulder height.
  • Clear worktops.
  • Good lighting.

Equipment

  • Perching stool.
  • Kitchen trolley.
  • Easy-grip utensils.
  • Jar and tin openers.

Using a kettle safely

  • Fill only with what you need.
  • A kettle tipper or lighter kettle can help.
  • Ask an OT if worried about burns.

What happens at an occupational therapy kitchen visit

  • An OT may watch you make a drink or simple meal.
  • Ask your council for a care needs assessment.
  • Be honest about what you find hard.
  • Ask about equipment and layout changes.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Will adaptations be free?

Small aids often are after assessment.

Can I buy my own?

Yes, but advice helps.
